---
title: "Quiz: decision trees"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A tree has three questions: "$x \le 0.5$?", then on both sides "$y \le 0.3$?". Into how many regions does it cut the plane, and what shape are they?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each question cuts one region in two, along an axis.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Four regions (one per leaf), all axis-aligned rectangles: left-bottom, left-top, right-bottom, right-top. Here both sides happen to use the same threshold on $y$, so the four rectangles form a $2 \times 2$ grid.
:::

---

**Q2.** A node holds 6 nuclei and 2 background pixels. What is its Gini impurity? What would a pure node have?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$G = 1 - 0.75^2 - 0.25^2 = 0.375$. A pure node (one class only) has $G = 0$; the most mixed two-class node has $G = 0.5$.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does the split search only try thresholds **between** neighbouring values of a feature?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What changes when the threshold moves between two neighbouring values?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Moving the threshold between two neighbouring values does not move any training point from one side to the other, so the split and its impurity stay the same. Only $n - 1$ distinct splits exist per feature for $n$ distinct values; taking the midpoint is a convention.
:::

---

**Q4.** A tree grown until every leaf is pure has 0 % training error. Why is that not good news?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does it do with a mislabelled or noisy training point?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It has memorised the training data, including its noise: every mislabelled point gets its own small region. On new data those regions are wrong, so the test error is higher than for a shallower tree. Zero training error says nothing about new data.
:::

---

**Q5.** You tried ten depths and chose the one with the smallest **test** error. What is wrong with reporting that test error?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What role did the test set play in the choice?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The test set was used to choose a setting, so it has become a validation set and its error is optimistic (the best of ten noisy numbers). Choose on a validation set or by cross-validation, then evaluate once on a test set that played no role in any choice.
:::

---

**Q6.** In 5-fold cross-validation, how often is each training example used for validation, and how many trees are grown per setting?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each fold takes its turn.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each example is validated exactly once (when its fold is held out) and used for training in the other 4 rounds. Five trees are grown per setting, one per round; their 5 validation errors are averaged.
:::

---

**Q7.** One feature is an area in µm², another an intensity from 0 to 4095. Do you have to rescale them before growing a tree?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does a split depend on the size of the numbers or on their order?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. A split only depends on the order of the values along one feature; rescaling (or any increasing transformation) moves the thresholds but keeps the same splits. Methods based on distances (nearest neighbour, the SVM) do need comparable scales.
:::

---

**Q8.** A regression tree with 4 leaves is fitted to a smooth intensity ramp. What does the fit look like?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a leaf predict?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A staircase of 4 flat steps: each leaf predicts the mean of its points, so the fit is piecewise constant. A smooth ramp needs many leaves to be approximated well.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that for two classes the Gini impurity is $2p(1-p)$, where $p$ is the share of one class.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$p_1 = p$, $p_2 = 1 - p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$G = 1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2 = 1 - p^2 - 1 + 2p - p^2 = 2p - 2p^2 = 2p(1-p)$. Equivalently $\sum_{k \ne l}p_kp_l = p(1-p) + (1-p)p$.
:::
